faq.title: Why does Airtel use Non-Standalone (NSA) while Jio uses Standalone (SA) 5G in India?
faq.description: Bharti Airtel possessed a mature, highly optimized nationwide 4G LTE network. Adopting 3GPP Option 3x (NSA) allowed Airtel to deploy 5G gNodeB radios on existing cell towers anchored to their 4G Evolved Packet Core (EPC), enabling fast rollout with lower upfront capital expenditure. Reliance Jio, lacking legacy 2G/3G network constraints, chose to build a greenfield 3GPP Option 2 (SA) network with a dedicated cloud-native 5G Core (5GC) from day one.

faq.title: Does 5G NSA drain smartphone battery faster than 5G SA?
faq.description: Yes. In an NSA deployment, your smartphone must maintain two simultaneous active radio frequency connections: an LTE anchor connection for signaling/control and an NR connection for user payload data (Dual Connectivity / EN-DC). Running two radio transceivers increases baseband power consumption by roughly 15% to 25% compared to pure SA single-radio operation.

faq.title: What is VoNR and why is it important for 5G users?
faq.description: VoNR (Voice over New Radio) is the 5G equivalent of VoLTE. On a 5G Standalone network, voice calls are routed directly over native 5G packet channels without dropping to 4G. On an NSA network, the phone must execute an EPS Fallback, momentarily dropping the signaling connection back to 4G LTE to complete the phone call, which can cause a 1-to-2 second call setup delay.

html:
The Indian 5G Revolution: Two Radically Different Philosophies

When the 5G spectrum auction concluded in India, the nation witnessed the fastest commercial cellular rollout in telecommunications history. Within months, hundreds of millions of subscribers across major metropolitan centers, tier-2 towns, and rural districts gained access to gigabit-class mobile internet speeds. However, despite both telecom operators marketing their services under the generic "5G" moniker, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel made fundamentally divergent architectural decisions at the physical and core network layers.

Reliance Jio invested tens of billions of dollars to construct a completely sovereign, greenfield 5G Standalone (SA) network. In stark contrast, Bharti Airtel opted for a 5G Non-Standalone (NSA) network architecture, leveraging their existing nationwide 4G LTE infrastructure. While both networks deliver impressive downlink speeds that routinely surpass 300 to 800 Mbps, the real-world performance characteristics—including call setup latency, battery consumption, indoor penetration, and future enterprise capabilities—are vastly different.

In this comprehensive technical treatise, we analyze the 3GPP architectural specifications behind 5G SA and NSA, demystify spectrum band allocations in India, examine the mechanics of Voice over New Radio (VoNR), and reveal how your smartphone's baseband modem behaves on each network.

Architectural Deep Dive: 3GPP Option 2 vs. Option 3x

To understand the difference between SA and NSA, we must examine the standards established by the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) in Release 15 and Release 16:

  • 5G Non-Standalone (Option 3x Architecture): In an NSA network, the cellular tower deploys new 5G New Radio (gNodeB) transceivers, but the underlying core network remains the legacy 4G Evolved Packet Core (EPC). Your smartphone establishes a primary control-plane connection to a 4G LTE anchor band (eNodeB) for network registration, mobility management, and paging. User-plane payload data is split between 4G and 5G radios via E-UTRA-NR Dual Connectivity (EN-DC). While this allows telecom operators to roll out 5G speeds instantly with minimal core infrastructure investment, it remains tethered to 4G routing constraints.
  • 5G Standalone (Option 2 Architecture): In a pure SA deployment, there is zero reliance on legacy 4G systems. The gNodeB radio access network connects directly to a modern, cloud-native 5G Core (5GC). The 5GC introduces a Service-Based Architecture (SBA) with virtualized network functions (User Plane Function UPF, Access and Mobility Management Function AMF, and Session Management Function SMF). This delivers true sub-10ms ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC), end-to-end network slicing, and native packet handling.

Comprehensive Comparison Matrix: Jio SA vs. Airtel NSA

3GPP Architecture Option 2 (Pure 5GC) Option 3x (EPC 4G Core Anchor)

Mid-Band Capacity 3300 MHz (Band n78) 3300 MHz (Band n78)

Network Slicing Support Native end-to-end dynamic slicing Not supported (Core network bound)

The Spectrum Battle: Why 700MHz (Band n28) Changes Everything

In wireless radio frequency (RF) physics, radio waves adhere to immutable electromagnetic propagation laws: higher frequencies provide massive data capacity but attenuate rapidly when striking solid obstacles, whereas lower frequencies penetrate deep into reinforced concrete buildings and travel tens of kilometers across open terrain.

This is where Jio's spectrum portfolio provides a massive structural advantage:

  • Jio's Secret Weapon (Band n28 - 700 MHz): Jio spent over Rs 39,000 crore to acquire 10MHz of paired spectrum in the pristine 700MHz frequency band nationwide. Because 700MHz sits in the sub-GHz range, its physical propagation allows 5G signals to effortlessly penetrate elevator shafts, underground basements, and dense concrete high-rises where high-frequency signals cannot reach. Even when you are deep indoors, your phone stays connected to native 5G.
  • Airtel's Dynamic Spectrum Sharing Strategy: Airtel chose not to purchase 700MHz spectrum, relying instead on its mid-band 3300MHz (n78) for 5G speed and leveraging legacy 1800MHz and 2100MHz bands via Dynamic Spectrum Sharing (DSS). While Airtel achieves phenomenal outdoor download speeds, users frequently notice their device dropping back to 4G LTE when stepping inside interior rooms or underground parking garages.

The Battery Dilemma: Why 5G NSA Drains More Power

One of the most persistent complaints among modern smartphone users is accelerated battery depletion when 5G is enabled. However, few realize that battery drain is heavily influenced by whether you are connected to an SA or NSA network:

  1. Dual-Transceiver Overhead (EN-DC): When your phone connects to Airtel's NSA network, its Qualcomm Snapdragon or MediaTek Dimensity baseband modem must keep two distinct radio chains energized. The receiver must continuously listen to the 4G LTE anchor cell for system control messages while simultaneously decoding high-frequency 5G NR carriers for streaming data. This dual-radio concurrent operation generates significant thermal heat and increases baseline modem power draw by 20% to 30%.
  2. Single-Carrier Standby in SA: On Jio's SA network, the smartphone modem operates in pure 5G mode. When the phone is idle in your pocket, only the 5G receiver monitors the paging channel, enabling deeper modem sleep cycles and reducing passive standby battery drain.
  3. Weak Signal Amplification: If an NSA signal is weak, the phone ramps up transmission wattage on BOTH the LTE and 5G radios to maintain the connection, dramatically compounding thermal load and battery drain.

VoNR vs. EPS Fallback: The Evolution of Mobile Voice Calls

Voice calling over cellular networks has undergone monumental evolutionary shifts: from circuit-switched 2G/3G calls to packet-based 4G VoLTE. 5G introduces the next phase: Voice over New Radio (VoNR).

  • EPS Fallback (NSA Mechanism): In an NSA network, because the 5G radio lacks an independent voice routing core, incoming or outgoing calls trigger an Evolved Packet System (EPS) Fallback. Your phone disconnects its 5G data carrier, falls back to 4G LTE VoLTE to negotiate the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) handshake, and completes the call. This introduces a noticeable 1.5 to 2.5 second delay before you hear the first ringback tone, and throttles your background download speeds during calls.
  • Native VoNR (Jio SA Mechanism): With VoNR enabled on Jio, voice packets are encoded using ultra-high-definition EVS (Enhanced Voice Services) audio codecs and transmitted directly across the 5G radio bearer. Call connection occurs in under 500 milliseconds, voice clarity is remarkably crisp, and high-speed 5G downloads continue uninterrupted in the background while you speak!

Network Slicing in Practice: Sovereign Radio Slices for Gaming & Enterprise

Beyond raw download speeds and VoNR voice clarity, the crowning architectural capability of pure 5G Standalone networks is end-to-end dynamic network slicing. In legacy 4G and 5G NSA networks, all subscriber traffic—whether a high-stakes competitive mobile multiplayer game, a streaming 4K video, or a casual background email sync—is dumped into the exact same best-effort network pipe. During massive public gatherings like cricket matches or music festivals, the cellular tower becomes congested, and gaming latency spikes uncontrollably from 25ms to over 300ms.

5G Standalone's cloud-native 5GC core completely solves this through software-defined radio virtualization:

  • Virtual Independent Networks: The telecom operator can partition physical radio spectrum and core routing into isolated virtual "slices". Each slice operates with dedicated QoS (Quality of Service) guarantees, guaranteed minimum throughput, and prioritized radio scheduling.
  • Ultra-Low-Latency Gaming Slices: A dedicated gaming slice can bypass congested public internet gateways, routing game packets directly to local Multi-Access Edge Computing (MEC) servers deployed at the base of the cell tower, locking latency to under 12 milliseconds regardless of how many thousands of people are streaming video on the same cell tower.
  • Emergency Services & Healthcare Priority: Network slicing allows first responders, ambulances, and remote robotic surgery streams to maintain mission-critical, unthrottled communication bandwidth even if consumer networks suffer severe localized congestion during natural disasters.

Overcoming 5G Signal Dead Zones: VoWiFi Handover Mechanics

Because high-frequency 5G signals (especially mid-band 3300MHz) face significant physical attenuation when penetrating thick concrete exterior walls, users frequently encounter localized indoor dead zones. Both Jio and Airtel solve this indoor coverage limitation through seamless Voice over Wi-Fi (VoWiFi) and Wi-Fi Calling Handover:

  • Dual-Registration Architecture: When connected to home or office broadband, your smartphone establishes an encrypted IPsec tunnel directly into the telecom operator's core network (ePDG / N3IWF gateways).
  • Zero-Interruption Radio Handover: If you walk out of your house while actively talking on a VoWiFi call, the baseband modem monitors signal attenuation. As Wi-Fi signal drops below -82 dBm, the network executes a seamless, zero-drop handover directly to the cellular 5G VoNR or 4G VoLTE bearer without terminating your call or dropping voice packets.

How to Audit Your 5G Connection Type on Android

Curious whether your Android smartphone is currently connected to 5G SA or NSA? You can perform a diagnostic inspection using Android's native engineering screens:

  1. Open your phone's dialer app and enter the engineering code: *#*#4636#*#*.
  2. Tap Phone information.
  3. Scroll down to the NR State field:
    • If it reads NR_STATE_CONNECTED with SA mode, you are on pure Standalone 5G.
    • If it reads NR_STATE_RESTRICTED or lists an active LTE anchor with dual-carrier (EN-DC), you are connected to Non-Standalone 5G.
  4. Alternatively, install the open-source diagnostic utility NetMonster from F-Droid or Google Play to view real-time cell tower IDs, active carrier frequencies (e.g., n28 + n78), and signal strength (RSRP/RSRQ).

The Verdict: Which 5G Experience is Superior?

The choice between 5G SA and NSA is not a matter of one being "good" and the other "bad"—they represent different engineering trade-offs. Bharti Airtel's NSA network delivered immediate nationwide availability with exceptional outdoor peak throughput by capitalizing on existing 4G infrastructure. However, as 5G ecosystems mature in 2026, Reliance Jio's massive investment in pure Standalone (SA) architecture and 700MHz low-band spectrum provides superior indoor signal resilience, lower latency, native VoNR calling, and reduced modem battery strain. For modern users, having a smartphone with comprehensive sub-GHz and mid-band 5G band support is essential to enjoying the true promise of next-generation wireless connectivity.
